screens.title: The 'from' statement — definition and role
screens.narratorSegment: The 'from' statement defines the exact criteria a route must satisfy for a routing policy term to execute its action. Think of it as a checklist: every condition you list inside that 'from' must be true for the term to match. For example, if a term contains from protocol bgp and from neighbor 192.0.2.5, a route must be learned via BGP and from that neighbor to match. This AND logic is often misunderstood — learners sometimes expect an OR behavior, which leads to unexpected policy outcomes. A concrete example: to accept only BGP routes from a specific peer, include both protocol bgp and neighbor in the same term; omitting protocol might accept routes that carry that neighbor address but are learned by a different protocol in unusual setups. Another real-world scenario is exporting internal prefixes only when a route originated from a specific interface and has a community tag; both conditions must be present. Key misconception: people sometimes place mutually exclusive conditions in the same term, making the term never match. Key takeaway: list the minimal, consistent set of conditions required for the behavior you want, and prefer separate terms for logically different cases so errors are easier to spot. How would you split conditions if you needed multiple matching behaviors?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: All conditions inside a single 'from' are ANDed; the term matches only when every condition is true.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Definition
'from' statement
Specifies the conditions a route must meet for the policy term to apply.
Definition
Every condition inside a 'from' is evaluated together; the term matches only if all are true.
Misconception
Do not assume 'from' items are ORed. If you need OR behavior, create multiple terms each with its own from.
Key Takeaway

Use separate terms for distinct match sets; keep 'from' clauses logically consistent to avoid never-matching terms.

Concrete example
set policy-options policy-statement IMPORT-BGP
 set term only-from-peer from protocol bgp
 set term only-from-peer from neighbor 192.0.2.5
 set term only-from-peer then accept
This term matches only BGP routes learned from 192.0.2.5.
Check your understanding
  • Would a route learned from OSPF with neighbor 192.0.2.5 match the example above? No.
  • How do you implement OR logic for two different neighbors? Create two terms each matching a neighbor.

screens.title: route-filter match types
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding route-filter match types is essential when you target destination prefixes. 'exact' matches a single prefix and length, for example 192.168.1.0/24 exact will match only that /24. 'longer' and 'orlonger' include that prefix and any more specific prefixes beneath it, so a route-filter 192.168.1.0/24 longer catches 192.168.1.0/25 and other more-specific subnets. 'upto' restricts matches to prefixes within a maximum mask length — route-filter 192.168.0.0/16 upto /24 matches anything between /16 and /24 inclusive, but not /25. The prefix-length-range form is similar but lets you specify a specific inclusive range such as /20-/24. A concrete example: to match all 172.16.0.0/16 prefixes with masks between /20 and /24 you would use prefix-length-range /20-/24. A common mistake is choosing 'longer' when you intended 'upto' or vice versa, causing over- or under-inclusion. Always test with show route detail and with realistic route sets in a lab. Key takeaway: pick the smallest match type that covers the prefixes you intend and validate with route output. route-filter match types means pick exact for single lengths, longer/orlonger for more-specifics, upto or prefix-length-range to bound length inclusively.. In practical terms, exact, longer, orlonger, upto, and prefix-length-range explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › route-filter Match Types
Match type comparison
Choose the match that maps to your intended prefix set.
exact
Matches exactly the given prefix and length. Use when you want a single prefix only.
longer / orlonger
Include the base prefix and all more-specifics beneath it. Good for catching subnets.
upto
Match prefixes up to a specified maximum length, inclusive of the base length.
prefix-length-range
Specify an explicit inclusive length range, such as /20-/24, for precise control.
Key Takeaway

Match types determine which specific or aggregated prefixes are included; select the one that minimizes unintended matches and validate in a lab.

Concrete examples
route-filter 192.168.1.0/24 exact
route-filter 192.168.1.0/24 longer
route-filter 192.168.0.0/16 upto /24
route-filter 172.16.0.0/16 prefix-length-range /20-/24
Try each against a sample route table to see which prefixes would match.
Common mistake
Using longer when you intended upto can include more-specific prefixes you did not plan to affect. Conversely, using exact when you intended a range will under-match.

screens.title: Using prefix-lists for reuse
screens.narratorSegment: Prefix-lists are a simple way to group non-contiguous prefixes and reference them from multiple policy statements. Instead of repeating several route-filter lines in many terms, you define prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS under policy-options and add each prefix once. This improves readability and reduces typos. For example, set policy-options prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS 10.0.0.0/8 and then reference it with set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT-INTERNAL from prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS. A practical process is: first plan the logical groups of prefixes you need to match, second define prefix-lists under policy-options, third reference them from terms, and finally test with show route for a sample prefix to ensure the membership behaves as expected. A common misconception is thinking prefix-lists automatically apply length semantics; they simply list prefixes you want to match. If you need length ranges, use route-filter forms inside terms or include multiple entries in the prefix-list. Key takeaway: prefix-lists simplify policy statements and centralize prefix definitions so corrections are made in one place rather than many. Using prefix-lists for reuse means they make policies cleaner, reduce repetition, and centralize prefix management; use route-filter when you need length-range semantics.. In practical terms, define once, reference many to improve clarity and maintenance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Prefix-list Process
Define & reference prefix-lists
A four-step process to build maintainable prefix matches.
1
Plan groups
Decide which prefixes belong together for policy purposes.
2
Define under policy-options
Create prefix-list entries once for reuse in many terms.
3
Reference in terms
Use from prefix-list NAME inside your policy-statement terms.
4
Test and adjust
Validate with show route to ensure routes you expect are included.
Key Takeaway

Use prefix-lists to centralize prefix definitions and reduce the chance of typos across multiple policy terms.

Code snippet
set policy-options prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS 10.0.0.0/8
set policy-options prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS 172.16.0.0/16
set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT-INTERNAL from prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS
Define once, reference many. Prefix-lists are literal prefix members; use route-filter for length ranges.
Common misconception
Assuming a prefix-list entry implies length filtering. If you need ranges, use route-filter prefix-length-range or include multiple entries explicitly.

screens.title: Protocol-based matches
screens.narratorSegment: Matching by protocol lets you treat whole families of routes differently depending on where they originated. The protocol keyword accepts values such as ospf, bgp, static, direct, and aggregate. For example, you might accept every OSPF route into your routing table but apply stricter filtering for BGP-sourced routes from external peers. A concrete scenario: you want to accept OSPF routes unconditionally into an import policy. Create a term with from protocol ospf and then accept. In contrast, BGP routes often carry attributes you want to inspect first, so you might match protocol bgp and then test as-path or community before accepting. A common misconception is expecting protocol matching to identify the neighbor; it does not. Protocol identifies how the route was learned, not which peer provided it. If you need both, include both from protocol bgp and from neighbor in the same term. When combining protocol with prefix filters be sure the conditions are logically consistent — a route learned via static cannot simultaneously have protocol bgp. Key takeaway: use protocol matches to broadly separate route treatment, then refine with other attributes when necessary.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Protocol Match
Protocol matches
Separate treatment based on how a route was learned.
Examples
from protocol ospf — accept internal OSPF routes; from protocol bgp — apply BGP attribute checks.
Misconception
Protocol does not imply neighbor identity. If you need a specific peer, also use from neighbor.
Key Takeaway

Protocol matches are effective for broad classification; refine decisions with additional attributes for precision.

Concrete scenario
set policy-options policy-statement IMPORT-OSPF-ONLY
 set term accept-ospf from protocol ospf
 set term accept-ospf then accept
 set term reject-all-others then reject
This policy accepts only routes learned via OSPF and rejects all others.
Check
After applying, use show route protocol ospf and show route <prefix> detail to confirm expected matches.

screens.title: Neighbor and as-path matching
screens.narratorSegment: BGP routing policies often need to be peer-aware. The neighbor match lets you match routes based on the specific BGP peer IP; this is typically used in import policies where behavior differs per peer. For example, set policy-options policy-statement IMPORT-FROM-PEER from neighbor 192.0.2.1 will match routes learned from that IP. The as-path match operates on the AS path attribute and is usually backed by global as-path definitions created under policy-options. An as-path definition uses regular expressions to describe path shapes — for instance, a pattern that ends with 65000 can be written as a global object and then referenced. A concrete example: define set policy-options as-path MY-AS-PATH ".* 65000$" and then from as-path MY-AS-PATH. A critical caution: AS-path regex are powerful but easy to get wrong; an incorrect regex can over-match and filter many routes. Always test regexes in a safe environment. Misconception: neighbor matching is not a substitute for AS-path checks; they serve different purposes. Key takeaway: match by neighbor when the peer identity matters, and use as-path for path-based selection, testing regex carefully before deployment. Neighbor and as-path matching means use neighbor to target specific peers and as-path to target routes by their as path; test regex patterns carefully.. In practical terms, target routes from particular peers or as path patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Neighbor & AS-path
Neighbor vs AS-path
Peer identity and path patterns are complementary criteria for BGP policy.
Neighbor example
from neighbor 192.0.2.1 — use for peer-specific import or export behavior.
AS-path example
Define as-path regex under policy-options and reference it: set policy-options as-path MY-AS-PATH ".* 65000$" then from as-path MY-AS-PATH.
Safety note
Test AS-path regex thoroughly. A mistaken pattern can affect many routes and cause routing issues.
Key Takeaway

Use neighbor for peer-specific decisions and as-path for route selection by path characteristics; always test regexes before committing.

Code snippets
set policy-options policy-statement IMPORT-FROM-PEER from neighbor 192.0.2.1

set policy-options as-path MY-AS-PATH ".* 65000$"
set policy-options policy-statement FILTER-AS from as-path MY-AS-PATH
Define the as-path object globally then reference it inside your term.
Misconception check
If you need both peer identity and path shape, include neighbor and as-path together in the same term; both must be true for a match.

screens.title: Community and origin matches
screens.narratorSegment: Communities and origin attributes are additional tools to refine BGP policy. Communities act as tags attached to routes that can be matched across AS boundaries when configured as optional transitive attributes. For example, set a community NO-EXPORT members no-export and then match it with from community NO-EXPORT in a policy to prevent exporting those routes. Origin matches inspect the origin attribute — igp, egp, or incomplete — and allow you to prefer or restrict routes based on how they were injected into BGP. A concrete example: use from origin igp to prefer routes that originated from an interior IGP. A common mistake is failing to define the community object globally or mis-typing its name, which results in a term that never matches. Another misconception is assuming communities are always preserved across neighbors; some provider configurations strip or rewrite communities, so verify end-to-end behavior. screens.title: Combining conditions and term order
screens.narratorSegment: Writing robust routing policies means thinking about both the conditions inside a term and the order of terms across the policy. Every 'from' within a single term is evaluated with logical AND, so combine only compatible conditions. To implement OR-like behavior, use separate terms: one term per OR case, ordered from most specific to least specific. For example, to export 192.168.10.0/24 to a specific neighbor but block it to others, create a term matching prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 and neighbor 10.0.0.1 with then accept, followed by a term matching prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 with then reject. The order is crucial: the specific accept must appear before the broader reject term. A common mistake is placing the reject before the accept, which makes the accept unreachable. Also remember that within-term condition order does not affect matching; it is the term ordering across the policy that resolves precedence. Key takeaway: design policies top-down from specific to general, and prefer clear separate terms rather than complex single terms with many ANDed conditions when you intend OR behavior. screens.title: Hands-on lab: export specific prefix to one BGP neighbor
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the hands-on scenario from the chapter: you want to advertise 192.168.10.0/24 only to neighbor 10.0.0.1 and ensure other peers do not receive it. First, enter configuration mode on a Junos CLI. Define a prefix-list named INTERNAL-NET-10 with the exact /24 entry. Then create a policy-statement EXPORT-SPECIFIC-TO-PEER with a term that matches the prefix-list and neighbor 10.0.0.1 and accepts that term. Add a second term that matches the same prefix-list and rejects it for others; place this after the specific accept term. Finally add a default-accept to permit other routes to be exported. After committing, verify with show route 192.168.10.0/24 detail and with show route protocol bgp to confirm whether the route is being advertised or blocked as intended. A common error is placing the reject term before the accept term, which prevents the desired accept. Another is forgetting to define the prefix-list under policy-options, making the from prefix-list condition ineffective. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Task steps
Follow these steps in the Junos CLI to implement the scenario safely.
  1. Enter configuration mode: edit.
  2. Define the prefix-list under policy-options for 192.168.10.0/24 exact.
  3. Create policy-statement EXPORT-SPECIFIC-TO-PEER.
  4. Add term allow-10-to-peer with from prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 and from neighbor 10.0.0.1, then accept.
  5. Add term deny-10-to-others matching prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 then reject, placed after the specific term.
  6. Add a default-accept term to allow other routes to export if desired and commit.
  7. Verify using show route 192.168.10.0/24 detail and show route protocol bgp.
Key Takeaway

Define objects before referencing them, place specific terms first, and validate with show route commands.

Starter configuration template
edit policy-options
set prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 192.168.10.0/24 exact

edit policy-options policy-statement EXPORT-SPECIFIC-TO-PEER
set term allow-10-to-peer from prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10
set term allow-10-to-peer from neighbor 10.0.0.1
set term allow-10-to-peer then accept
set term deny-10-to-others from prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10
set term deny-10-to-others then reject
set term default-accept then accept
up
commit and-quit
Use this template in a simulated environment before applying to production.
Common pitfalls
Placing deny before allow, forgetting to define the prefix-list, or typos in object names — all lead to terms that never match as intended.

screens.title: Verifying matches and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the step that catches mistakes before they become outages. After you configure a policy, use commands like show route detail to inspect the selected route’s attributes — protocol, next hop, AS path, and community — so you can tell whether your 'from' conditions should match. show route protocol lists routes learned by a specific protocol and helps verify broad protocol-based filters. If a term doesn't match as expected, check for typos in referenced object names, confirm the prefix-list or as-path exists under policy-options, and validate that communities or AS path attributes are present on the route. Another useful technique is to create a temporary accept-only policy and apply it in a read-only test environment to observe matches without disrupting live traffic. A common troubleshooting mistake is assuming a missing match means the policy is wrong — sometimes the route simply lacks the attribute you expected, such as a community being stripped upstream. Key takeaway: verify route attributes first, then your policy; fix object definitions and term order before changing production policies. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Mistakes in match conditions are common but largely preventable with disciplined practices. First, incorrect route-filter match types are frequent — using exact when you meant longer or prefix-length-range when upto would be appropriate. Always choose the operator that best describes the prefix set you expect. Second, typos in prefix-list, as-path, or community names render conditions ineffective; verify object names with show configuration | display set. Third, forgetting to define global objects under policy-options means the term will never match. Fourth, overly broad matches can accidentally capture routes you didn't intend to change, while overly specific matches can miss routes you intended to affect. A practical strategy is to test incremental changes: apply a policy in a lab, use show route detail to confirm matches, and then deploy. Another useful habit is to write clear, commented configuration snippets and centralize objects like prefix-lists to reduce repetition. Key takeaway: plan, define global objects first, test route attributes, and order terms from specific to general — these steps prevent most common failures. screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts from this chapter. Finally, always verify route attributes and test match logic in a lab to avoid common mistakes such as typos, incorrect match types, missing definitions, and term ordering errors. Keep these concepts in mind as you construct policies: precise matches, clear object definitions, correct term order, and verification are the foundation of safe routing policy management.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the Junos routing policy 'from' statement — the gatekeeper that decides whether a route triggers the actions you specify. You will learn how to match destination prefixes with route-filter and prefix-list, how to select routes by the protocol they were learned from, and how to use BGP attributes like neighbor, AS path, community, and origin to make precise policy decisions. We’ll show concrete examples such as matching a single /24 exactly, matching more-specific prefixes with 'longer' or 'orlonger', and limiting matches with a prefix-length-range. You will also see how prefix-lists improve reuse, why AS-path regex must be tested carefully, and why all 'from' conditions in a term are ANDed. A practical lab walkthrough is included so you can practice creating a prefix-list, writing terms that match a specific neighbor, and verifying results with show route output. By the end you will be able to design targeted import and export rules, avoid common pitfalls like typos or overly broad matches, and verify that your policy matches the routes you expect. Ready to begin with the core objectives and examples that follow?

These objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you will configure 'from' statements to match routes by destination prefix using route-filter and prefix-list. That means you can target single prefixes or ranges of prefix lengths with commands like route-filter 192.168.1.0/24 exact or using a named prefix-list. Second, you will match by protocol so you can accept or reject routes depending on whether they came from OSPF, BGP, static, or direct sources. This matters when you combine internal routing with external peers. Third, you will apply BGP-specific matches: neighbor, as-path, community, and origin. You will learn to define these objects globally and reference them in policy terms. Fourth, you will learn to identify and avoid common mistakes such as choosing the wrong route-filter match type or forgetting to define global objects. Each objective includes a short explanation and a mnemonic so you can recall the right tool when writing policies. Together these skills let you design precise import and export rules and verify them safely in a lab.

These secondary objectives sharpen how you apply match conditions in real deployments. You will create and reference prefix-lists for cleaner, reusable prefix matching instead of repeating route-filter lines. You will craft as-path and community objects under policy-options and reference them to make BGP decisions consistent across policies. You will also practice ordering terms correctly: place specific peer matches before broader matches so targeted behavior wins. Finally, you will learn testing and verification habits such as using show route protocol and show route detail to confirm which attributes a route carries. A concrete example: define a prefix-list for 10.0.0.0/8 and reference it in a term that accepts routes from a single neighbor while another term rejects the same prefix for other peers. A common misconception to avoid is assuming order of 'from' statements inside a term matters — they are all ANDed. Term order matters across the policy, but within a term every condition must be true. These skills reduce mistakes and improve policy predictability.

The 'from' statement defines the exact criteria a route must satisfy for a routing policy term to execute its action. Think of it as a checklist: every condition you list inside that 'from' must be true for the term to match. For example, if a term contains from protocol bgp and from neighbor 192.0.2.5, a route must be learned via BGP and from that neighbor to match. This AND logic is often misunderstood — learners sometimes expect an OR behavior, which leads to unexpected policy outcomes. A concrete example: to accept only BGP routes from a specific peer, include both protocol bgp and neighbor in the same term; omitting protocol might accept routes that carry that neighbor address but are learned by a different protocol in unusual setups. Another real-world scenario is exporting internal prefixes only when a route originated from a specific interface and has a community tag; both conditions must be present. Key misconception: people sometimes place mutually exclusive conditions in the same term, making the term never match. Key takeaway: list the minimal, consistent set of conditions required for the behavior you want, and prefer separate terms for logically different cases so errors are easier to spot. Understanding route-filter match types is essential when you target destination prefixes. 'exact' matches a single prefix and length, for example 192.168.1.0/24 exact will match only that /24. 'longer' and 'orlonger' include that prefix and any more specific prefixes beneath it, so a route-filter 192.168.1.0/24 longer catches 192.168.1.0/25 and other more-specific subnets. 'upto' restricts matches to prefixes within a maximum mask length — route-filter 192.168.0.0/16 upto /24 matches anything between /16 and /24 inclusive, but not /25. The prefix-length-range form is similar but lets you specify a specific inclusive range such as /20-/24. A concrete example: to match all 172.16.0.0/16 prefixes with masks between /20 and /24 you would use prefix-length-range /20-/24. A common mistake is choosing 'longer' when you intended 'upto' or vice versa, causing over- or under-inclusion. Always test with show route detail and with realistic route sets in a lab. Key takeaway: pick the smallest match type that covers the prefixes you intend and validate with route output. route-filter match types means pick exact for single lengths, longer/orlonger for more-specifics, upto or prefix-length-range to bound length inclusively.. Prefix-lists are a simple way to group non-contiguous prefixes and reference them from multiple policy statements. Instead of repeating several route-filter lines in many terms, you define prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS under policy-options and add each prefix once. This improves readability and reduces typos. For example, set policy-options prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS 10.0.0.0/8 and then reference it with set policy-options policy-statement EXPORT-INTERNAL from prefix-list MY-INTERNAL-NETS. A practical process is: first plan the logical groups of prefixes you need to match, second define prefix-lists under policy-options, third reference them from terms, and finally test with show route for a sample prefix to ensure the membership behaves as expected. A common misconception is thinking prefix-lists automatically apply length semantics; they simply list prefixes you want to match. If you need length ranges, use route-filter forms inside terms or include multiple entries in the prefix-list. Key takeaway: prefix-lists simplify policy statements and centralize prefix definitions so corrections are made in one place rather than many. Matching by protocol lets you treat whole families of routes differently depending on where they originated. The protocol keyword accepts values such as ospf, bgp, static, direct, and aggregate. For example, you might accept every OSPF route into your routing table but apply stricter filtering for BGP-sourced routes from external peers. A concrete scenario: you want to accept OSPF routes unconditionally into an import policy. Create a term with from protocol ospf and then accept. In contrast, BGP routes often carry attributes you want to inspect first, so you might match protocol bgp and then test as-path or community before accepting. A common misconception is expecting protocol matching to identify the neighbor; it does not. Protocol identifies how the route was learned, not which peer provided it. If you need both, include both from protocol bgp and from neighbor in the same term. When combining protocol with prefix filters be sure the conditions are logically consistent — a route learned via static cannot simultaneously have protocol bgp. Key takeaway: use protocol matches to broadly separate route treatment, then refine with other attributes when necessary.

BGP routing policies often need to be peer-aware. The neighbor match lets you match routes based on the specific BGP peer IP; this is typically used in import policies where behavior differs per peer. For example, set policy-options policy-statement IMPORT-FROM-PEER from neighbor 192.0.2.1 will match routes learned from that IP. The as-path match operates on the AS path attribute and is usually backed by global as-path definitions created under policy-options. An as-path definition uses regular expressions to describe path shapes — for instance, a pattern that ends with 65000 can be written as a global object and then referenced. A concrete example: define set policy-options as-path MY-AS-PATH ".* 65000$" and then from as-path MY-AS-PATH. A critical caution: AS-path regex are powerful but easy to get wrong; an incorrect regex can over-match and filter many routes. Always test regexes in a safe environment. Misconception: neighbor matching is not a substitute for AS-path checks; they serve different purposes. Key takeaway: match by neighbor when the peer identity matters, and use as-path for path-based selection, testing regex carefully before deployment. Neighbor and as-path matching means use neighbor to target specific peers and as-path to target routes by their as path; test regex patterns carefully.. Communities and origin attributes are additional tools to refine BGP policy. Communities act as tags attached to routes that can be matched across AS boundaries when configured as optional transitive attributes. For example, set a community NO-EXPORT members no-export and then match it with from community NO-EXPORT in a policy to prevent exporting those routes. Origin matches inspect the origin attribute — igp, egp, or incomplete — and allow you to prefer or restrict routes based on how they were injected into BGP. A concrete example: use from origin igp to prefer routes that originated from an interior IGP. A common mistake is failing to define the community object globally or mis-typing its name, which results in a term that never matches. Another misconception is assuming communities are always preserved across neighbors; some provider configurations strip or rewrite communities, so verify end-to-end behavior. Key takeaway: use community and origin matches when attributes are intentionally set and propagated; always confirm community propagation and object definitions before relying on them. Writing robust routing policies means thinking about both the conditions inside a term and the order of terms across the policy. Every 'from' within a single term is evaluated with logical AND, so combine only compatible conditions. To implement OR-like behavior, use separate terms: one term per OR case, ordered from most specific to least specific. For example, to export 192.168.10.0/24 to a specific neighbor but block it to others, create a term matching prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 and neighbor 10.0.0.1 with then accept, followed by a term matching prefix-list INTERNAL-NET-10 with then reject. The order is crucial: the specific accept must appear before the broader reject term. A common mistake is placing the reject before the accept, which makes the accept unreachable. Also remember that within-term condition order does not affect matching; it is the term ordering across the policy that resolves precedence. Key takeaway: design policies top-down from specific to general, and prefer clear separate terms rather than complex single terms with many ANDed conditions when you intend OR behavior. Add a second term that matches the same prefix-list and rejects it for others; place this after the specific accept term. Finally add a default-accept to permit other routes to be exported. Mistakes in match conditions are common but largely preventable with disciplined practices. First, incorrect route-filter match types are frequent — using exact when you meant longer or prefix-length-range when upto would be appropriate. Always choose the operator that best describes the prefix set you expect. Second, typos in prefix-list, as-path, or community names render conditions ineffective; verify object names with show configuration | display set. Third, forgetting to define global objects under policy-options means the term will never match. Fourth, overly broad matches can accidentally capture routes you didn't intend to change, while overly specific matches can miss routes you intended to affect. A practical strategy is to test incremental changes: apply a policy in a lab, use show route detail to confirm matches, and then deploy. Another useful habit is to write clear, commented configuration snippets and centralize objects like prefix-lists to reduce repetition. Key takeaway: plan, define global objects first, test route attributes, and order terms from specific to general — these steps prevent most common failures. Let's summarize the essential concepts from this chapter. First, the 'from' statement is the part of a routing policy term that defines conditions a route must meet; all conditions inside are ANDed. Second, route-filter match types control prefix inclusion — exact, longer/orlonger, upto, and prefix-length-range are the primary tools for defining prefix scopes. Third, prefix-lists centralize sets of prefixes for reuse and readability. Fourth, protocol matching lets you treat route families differently based on how they were learned. Fifth, BGP-specific matches — neighbor, as-path, community, and origin — provide fine-grained control but require global object definitions and careful testing. Finally, always verify route attributes and test match logic in a lab to avoid common mistakes such as typos, incorrect match types, missing definitions, and term ordering errors. Keep these concepts in mind as you construct policies: precise matches, clear object definitions, correct term order, and verification are the foundation of safe routing policy management.

Three compact reminders to carry forward: first, 'from' behavior is AND — every listed condition must be true. Second, choose route-filter operators carefully; exact, longer, orlonger, upto, and prefix-length-range each have distinct semantics that determine which prefix lengths match. Third, define prefix-list, as-path, and community objects under policy-options and reference them to reduce repetition and avoid typos. These simple rules help you design clear, maintainable routing policies that behave predictably when deployed. Before committing changes, inspect route attributes with show route detail and test policy logic in a lab to prevent accidental route leakage or unintended rejects.
